olm8ij-g52840-d1e103.summary: Rubric: Question 2, 'On the irascible and the concupiscible'.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e112.summary: States the question: whether, in the rational appetite, the irascible and concupiscible are distinguished as different powers. The printed text says 'appetitu naturali', but the argument and what follows show that the intellective appetite is meant. Opening argument for yes: the fitting (conveniens) and the arduous are different formal aspects of objects, and different formal objects show different powers. Confirmation: they are distinguished this way in the sensitive appetite, so by likeness also in the intellective.
claims: The fitting and the arduous are distinct formal objects.
Diversity of formal objects argues for diversity of powers.
Irascible and concupiscible are distinct in the sensitive appetite.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e134.summary: Argument in the opposite direction, followed by the plan of the reply. The will is a higher power than the sensitive appetite, and what is dispersed in lower things is united in higher ones, so the will is not divided into two powers. Aureol announces four points: that the irascible and concupiscible are distinguished; by what; where (in the sensitive or rational appetite); and whether as distinct powers.
claims: What is dispersed in inferior things is united in superior ones.
The will is a higher power than the sensitive appetite.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e158.summary: Table of the articles: (1) whether irascible and concupiscible are distinguished; (2) by what they are distinguished; (3) where they are distinguished. The question of whether they are distinct powers is handled in the third.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e186.summary: Rubric for Article 1: whether the irascible and concupiscible are distinguished.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e193.summary: Aureol affirms that the irascible and concupiscible are distinguished in some way, since all doctors say so. He cites Avicenna (De anima, part 4): the branches of the appetitive power are the irascible, whose role is to conquer, and the concupiscible, which desires. He also cites John Damascene (book II, ch. 12), drawing on Aristotle's division of the soul into a part obedient to reason and a part disobedient to it, and the pseudo-Augustinian De spiritu et anima on rationality, concupiscibility and irascibility as the whole structure of the soul.
claims: The irascible and concupiscible are distinguished in some manner.
There is consensus among authorities on this distinction.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e245.summary: Rubric for Article 2: by what the irascible and concupiscible are distinguished.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e254.summary: Plan of Article 2: first five ways of explaining the distinction, then Aureol's own view.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e263.summary: First way: the concupiscible inclines to the fitting, the irascible rises against or attacks what impedes. Argument: the perfection found in natural forms should be found even more in animal and living forms. Natural forms both tend toward what is fitting and resist what hinders. Fire, by the same power, rises and resists obstacles. Avicenna is cited in support.
claims: The concupiscible tends toward the fitting; the irascible resists the impeding.
Natural forms both tend to the fitting and resist impediments.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e293.summary: Further support for the first way from common sayings: the irascible is the champion of the concupiscible, and the passions of the irascible arise from those of the concupiscible.
claims: The irascible defends the concupiscible.
Irascible passions arise from concupiscible passions.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e304.summary: Rebuttal of the first way's conclusion. A natural form inclines and repels by the same power and act: a heavy stone descends and pushes aside every obstacle by the same weight and motion. So a fortiori the soul would incline and repel by the same power. What is united in lower things will be even more united in higher ones.
claims: A natural form inclines and repels by one and the same power and act.
Hence the analogy from nature supports one power, not two.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e330.summary: Second rebuttal of the first way. A dividing difference that constitutes a nature must cover every case of that species. Resisting does not hold of every act of the irascible, and the first way rests on the mistaken assumption that being angry is the act that fully defines the irascible. The text is corrupt in places.
claims: A constitutive dividing difference must apply to every member of the species.
Being angry is not the act that fully defines the irascible.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e356.summary: Second way: the powers differ by their objects. The concupiscible regards the good simply, the irascible the arduous good, as common speech says that one is angered about something arduous.
claims: The concupiscible regards the good simply; the irascible the arduous good.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e374.summary: Aureol grants that the second way is the common opinion and closer to the truth than the first, but finds it insufficient. Two differences that divide something common should not each be found within the domain of the other. Yet the concupiscible tends toward the arduous, and the irascible toward simple, non-arduous evil.
claims: The common opinion is closer to the truth but insufficient.
Differences dividing a genus should not be found crosswise in each other's domain.
The concupiscible is borne toward the arduous.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e392.summary: Arguments against the second way. One desires beatitude, which is arduous. The same power that is borne to something simply is borne to it in any degree, as the intellect to being and to particular being. The arduous is not a degree of goodness but only a difficult good, and one desires beatitude however difficult it is. A power capable of one act is capable of every act of the same kind, and desiring an arduous good is not a different kind of act from desiring a good simply. Conversely, one is angry at what is not arduous, such as a buzzing fly or Jonah at the ivy. Against the reply that whatever one is angry at is arduous to oneself: such things are easily overcome.
claims: Beatitude is an arduous good desired by the concupiscible.
The arduous is not a degree of goodness but a difficult good.
Desiring an arduous good is not a different kind of act from desiring a good simply.
Anger can be directed at non-arduous evils.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e448.summary: A further point against the second way: fear concerns a much greater evil, so the distinction by simple good and arduous good is not absolutely true.
claims: The distinction between simple and arduous good does not hold absolutely.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e455.summary: Third way: the powers are distinguished as intense and remiss. On this view an act of the irascible is just an intense act of the concupiscible. Hope is vehement desire, and fear when vehement belongs to the irascible.
claims: On the third way, irascible acts are intensified concupiscible acts.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e473.summary: Rebuttal of the third way: more and less intensity do not change the species, yet hope and desire for a good differ in species.
claims: Degree of intensity does not change species.
Hope and desire differ in species.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e482.summary: Further rebuttal. Hope is not vehement desire, because intense desire can coexist with despair, and what can coexist with the opposite of something is not identical with it. Similarly for the irascible: intense desire for revenge can exist without anger. One may desire revenge and not rise to it, while the angry person does rise, so desire for revenge and anger are separable.
claims: Intense desire can coexist with despair, so hope is not intense desire.
Desire for revenge is separable from anger.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e506.summary: Final argument against the third way: cause and effect are not the same, and hope, despair and the like arise from desire. Aureol refers to a fuller treatment in his Book III question on whether there was true sorrow in Christ.
claims: Hope and despair are effects of desire and so distinct from it.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e517.summary: Fourth way: the powers are distinguished by good and evil. The irascible concerns present evil, since no one is angry at food or pleasant things, while concupiscence concerns only the good. Aureol judges this the weakest view, because the irascible also concerns the good, as do hope and despair.
claims: The fourth way is the weakest, because the irascible also regards the good.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e544.summary: Fifth way: each power is named from the act that fully defines it, being angry for the irascible and desiring for the concupiscible. Aureol rejects this. An act that fully defines a power is predicated of every act of that power, as understanding is of every act of the intellect. But being proud, fearing and hoping are not being angry.
claims: An act that fully defines a power is predicated of every act of that power.
Being angry is not predicated of every irascible act.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e568.summary: Answers how the power can be named from the act of anger if that act does not fully define it. It is named from a prior or better-known act, as concupiscence is from desiring. Aureol then turns to his own view.
claims: A power can be named from its prior or better-known act.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e581.summary: Principle of Aureol's own account. When a power's acts fall into coordinated groups, each reducible to one general mode that is first and not further reducible, powers are distinguished by those modes. Examples are the opposed pairs desire and flight, delight and sorrow, hope and despair, and the way hearing and seeing are distinct groups of acts. Such groups are found here, so the distinction of powers follows.
claims: Powers are distinguished by irreducible general modes to which coordinated groups of acts reduce.
Hearing and seeing exemplify distinct groups of acts grounding distinct powers.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e629.summary: Identifies the two groups: one of being angry, hoping and despairing, daring and fearing; another of loving, desiring, delighting, hating, fleeing and being sad. The first group includes many acts of a different species from the second.
claims: The irascible group comprises anger, hope, despair, daring and fear.
The concupiscible group comprises love, desire, delight, hatred, flight and sorrow.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e647.summary: The acts within the first group differ in species among themselves but belong to one group because they agree in three respects: a common formal character, a common object-aspect, and a common causal mode. These three distinguish the whole group from the other.
claims: Acts of different species can belong to one group.
The irascible group is unified by a formal mode, an object-aspect and a causal mode.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e665.summary: First common feature: all acts of the irascible group consist in rising up, straining or being raised (assurgere, erigi). They are not formally acts of appetite: hope is rising toward an object one strains for, despair is failing to. Aureol states objections (anger is defined by appetite; willing and not willing cover every act of will) and holds that these acts are not formally appetition. Proof: hope is separable from desire. Someone who desires the papacy and then offends the cardinals despairs yet still desires it. Hope adds a rising up toward the object, based on a judgment that it can be obtained.
claims: Irascible acts are formally acts of rising up or straining, not of appetition.
Hope is separable from desire, as in desiring the papacy while despairing of it.
Hope is rising toward an object judged attainable.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e725.summary: Further proof. Desire comes and goes while anger continues: one may continually be angry at an enemy while only sometimes desiring their death. Similarly, the bold do not desire evil, and the fearful are cast down without desiring. So concupiscible acts such as desiring relate to the same object in one way, and irascible acts such as fear in another.
claims: Anger can persist while desire for revenge varies.
Daring and fear are not forms of desire.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e754.summary: Objections: what distinguishes these acts is not something added to appetite but bodily passions arising from desire. Straining is not a vital act in the body, so putting it in the rational appetite is irrational. And straining is just a circumstance of the act of desiring. Aureol says the first objection helps him: if bodily passions follow the acts, there must be something beyond desire that causes them.
claims: The bodily passions that follow appetitive acts presuppose something beyond desire that causes them.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e791.summary: Completes the reply to the first objection. When a cause is posited, its effect follows. Desire alone does not produce inflammation, so there must be something beyond desire, namely straining or rising up, from which the bodily passion first arises.
claims: Desire alone does not produce the bodily heat of anger.
Straining or rising up is the proximate cause of irascible bodily passion.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e809.summary: Reply to the second objection. Straining is a vital act of the appetite, not because it is life but because it includes a vital mode. The comparison is with understanding, which places its object in 'formed being', with sight and its species, and with love, by which one is borne intentionally to the beloved.
claims: Straining is a vital act of the appetite.
Vital acts proceed from life and include an intentional mode.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e831.summary: Second argument that straining is an act of appetite: what moves the appetite is its act, and the appetite is moved by straining or rising up. The external rational acts conform to the internal appetitive acts from which they arise or which they follow.
claims: Straining is an act of appetite because the appetite is moved by it.
External acts conform to the internal appetitive acts they follow.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e849.summary: Clarifies 'conform'. The external executive power is not raised in the same way. The appetite elicits an act by which it is raised intentionally, and a corresponding raising follows in the external executive power.
claims: The appetite's raising is intentional; the executive power's raising follows from it.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e868.summary: Reply to the third objection, that straining is a circumstance of the act and so cannot diversify powers. If straining means a degree within an act, it does not distinguish powers, but that is not Aureol's meaning. He means straining toward the object, a distinct act with its own mode, which does distinguish.
claims: Straining as a degree of an act does not distinguish powers.
Straining toward the object is a distinct act with its own mode.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e890.summary: Transition to the main objections against the claim that irascible acts are not formally appetition.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e899.summary: Answers the main objections and treats the second common feature, the object-aspect. Anger is not formally appetite for revenge, though it includes it. Being borne to an object may be appetition, but straining adds rising up. Willing and not willing cover all acts as they come from the appetite, but not the formal character of rising. Second feature: in the good, there is both the aspect of goodness and the aspect of arduousness. All irascible acts take arduousness as object, presupposing goodness. Aureol then asks what the arduous is. It is not merely absence (the blessed would lack 'tentio'), not excess (God would have no 'tentio'), and not value. He concludes that arduousness is relative to the one desiring: something, even if small, that is difficult for the appetite to attain.
claims: Anger includes but is not formally appetite for revenge.
Straining adds rising up beyond being borne toward an object.
All irascible acts take arduousness as their object, presupposing goodness.
The arduous is what is difficult to attain relative to the one desiring.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e980.summary: Refines the notion of the arduous. It does not signify impossibility relative to the desirer, since the impossible has no relation to attainability. It signifies what is possible to attain but only with difficulty. So it includes a certain height and elevation of the appetite, presupposing a common elevation.
claims: The arduous is the attainable with difficulty, not the impossible.
The arduous implies a height requiring elevation of the appetite.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e998.summary: Contrast of the two groups by object: the concupiscible group is borne to the good absolutely, the irascible group to arduousness. Rising, straining and being raised belong to the second group, and the height toward which one is raised is the formal aspect of the arduous.
claims: The concupiscible group regards the good absolutely; the irascible group regards arduousness.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1014.summary: Replies to objections about the arduous. If the arduous good is the absent good, in heaven there is no irascible act. 'Tentio' succeeds hope, but not in the same power, and follows intellect and will without any rising up. Alternatively, the arduous may be present but lofty. The arduous 'exceeds' in the sense of being attainable only with difficulty. This does not mean there are irascible acts in God. Example: a fly that offends you and escapes cannot easily be punished, so you rise up. The whole irascible group thus takes the arduous good as object and agrees in this object-aspect.
claims: The blessed have no irascible acts; tentio follows intellect and will.
The arduous exceeds in being attainable only with difficulty.
There are no irascible acts in God.
The whole irascible group agrees in having the arduous good as its object-aspect.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1067.summary: Third common feature, the causal mode. Aureol sets aside the objection that the arduous would be a relation. As willing includes intellectual apprehension and understanding includes imagination, so irascible acts include concupiscible acts. One is never angry without desiring revenge. Anger is a rising up that includes appetite for revenge, so there are two acts: a concupiscible desire, and an act of the other group directed to the height in which arduousness consists.
claims: Irascible acts include concupiscible acts as willing includes understanding.
Anger always includes desire for revenge.
Each irascible episode involves a concupiscible act and a distinct act of rising.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1102.summary: Extends the causal point to hope, fear and all irascible acts. One never hopes without desiring, then rises toward the object. All irascible acts include concupiscible ones, as willing includes understanding and understanding includes imagining. The reason is that the object of arduousness includes the good, to which the concupiscible first responds by desire.
claims: All irascible acts presuppose and include concupiscible acts.
The arduous object includes the good, which is first desired.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1128.summary: Conclusion of Article 2. The irascible and concupiscible are not distinguished by the arduous versus the good simply, which would wrongly stop the concupiscible from being borne toward a hoped-for arduous good. They are distinguished by mode: rising up or straining toward the desired good, versus being borne to the good simply. The distinction comes from the acts of different groups, each reducible to one general mode, and all passions reduce to these acts.
claims: The powers are distinguished not by object alone but by mode: straining versus being borne simply.
All passions reduce to the acts of these two groups.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1169.summary: Rubric for Article 3: where the irascible and concupiscible are distinguished.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1178.summary: Introduces Article 3. Across the two appetites, sensitive and rational, the irascible and concupiscible are certainly different powers. Whether they are distinguished within the same appetite is disputed.
claims: Sensitive and rational appetites are different powers.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1191.summary: First opinion, of an 'ancient doctor': the irascible and concupiscible are distinct powers in the sensitive appetite, but in the intellective appetite only by likeness.
claims: On the first opinion, the distinction holds properly only in the sensitive appetite.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1210.summary: Second opinion: in the sensitive appetite they are distinguished as two powers, in the intellective as two forces (vires) of the same power.
claims: On the second opinion, in the will they are distinct forces, not distinct powers.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1219.summary: First argument for the first opinion. A power whose fully proportioned object is a general aspect is not divided into several powers by the special aspects under that object. Powers whose proportioned objects are particular aspects are distinguished. Example: the common sense has all sensibles as object and is not divided, while sight and hearing are distinguished by colour and sound. Likewise the intellect has being in general. Minor premise: the intellective appetite is borne to the good in general, whereas the sensitive appetite regards the good and the arduous separately.
claims: A power with a general proportioned object is not divided by the special aspects under it.
Powers whose proportioned objects are particular aspects are distinct.
The intellective appetite regards the good in general.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1289.summary: Second argument for the first opinion. The intellective appetite relates to the sensitive appetites as the intellect relates to the sensitive cognitive powers. The intellect covers everything they do, so the intellective appetite covers all objects of the sensitive appetites and is not divided by them. Confirmation: what is dispersed below is united above.
claims: The intellective appetite relates to sensitive appetites as intellect to the senses.
What is dispersed in inferior things is united in superior ones.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1318.summary: Third argument for the first opinion, from authority. Philosophers (De anima III, Damascene citing Gregory Nazianzen) divide into irascible and concupiscible the appetite that is rational by participation. The will is rational by essence, not by participation. So the philosophers meant to divide only the sensitive appetite.
claims: The traditional division applies to the appetite rational by participation.
The will is rational by essence.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1344.summary: How the first opinion explains its position. The concupiscible's mode is to rest, the irascible's to repel rather than rest. These modes need different organs in the soul, and organic powers are distinguished by organs, so in the organic appetite they are two powers. The intellective appetite has no organ, so resting and repelling there are only directions of willing ('I will to rest', 'I will to repel'). The irascible and concupiscible are in the will only as sight and hearing are in the intellect when it judges colour and sound.
claims: The concupiscible's mode is resting; the irascible's is repelling.
Organic powers are distinguished by distinct organs.
The will, lacking an organ, contains the two only as directions of willing.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1394.summary: Transition: Aureol will argue first against the conclusion of the first opinion and then against its reasons.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1402.summary: Against the first argument's major premise. It is false unless the partial aspects are contained per se under the general aspect. Sight is borne per se to colour and so per se to whiteness, which falls per se under colour. It reaches substance only per accidens, since substance is extrinsic to colour. Aspects that are only accidentally related do argue different powers. The corrected major turns against the opponent: arduousness is not per se reducible to the good or the bad, so it argues a different power.
claims: Partial aspects fail to distinguish powers only if they are contained per se under the general object.
Sight reaches whiteness per se and substance per accidens.
Arduousness is not per se reducible to the aspect of good or bad.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1483.summary: Proof of the minor: according to Aristotle, the good is divided per se into the pleasant, the useful and the honourable, not into the arduous.
claims: The good is per se divided into pleasant, useful and honourable, not arduous.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1492.summary: Further proof. If the arduous were per se under good or bad, wherever there was arduousness there would be goodness or badness, as positing the lower posits the higher. But something audible can be arduous, meaning difficult and elevated, without being good or bad as such. So the power borne per se to arduousness differs from the power borne per se to the pleasant, useful or honourable good. For the irascible it is enough that its object be a desired good. Goodness is required as a precondition, not as its per se object.
claims: Arduousness can exist without goodness or badness as such.
The power borne per se to arduousness differs from that borne to the good.
Goodness is a precondition, not the per se object, of the irascible.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1523.summary: Against the first argument's minor, which has two readings. On the first, partial aspect means a species. Even if the rational appetite is borne to the good simply and the sensitive to a partial aspect, it does not follow that a power borne to arduousness must be another power.
claims: The first reading of the minor does not prove that arduousness requires a distinct power.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1554.summary: Second reading: partial aspect means a particular contained under a universal. Then the argument fails, because the same power is borne to the universal and the particular (colour and this colour). It would succeed only if it showed that the good and the arduous require distinct organs, which it does not.
claims: The same power is borne to a universal and its particulars.
The argument would work only if good and arduous required distinct organs.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1578.summary: Against the second and third arguments and the first opinion's account. If the intellect-appetite analogy worked, it would prove too much: the estimative power covers all sensitive apprehension, so there would be only one sensitive appetite. Against the third argument, Aristotle places the will among things rational by participation, since all moral virtues are in the will yet are said to be in the rational part by participation. De spiritu et anima places irascible and concupiscible in the soul before it enters the body. The account by resting and repelling fails because hope is irascible yet does not repel. Aureol reports Henry of Ghent (Quodlibet VIII, q.15): they are powers in the sensitive appetite and forces in the intellective. Henry places charity in the concupiscible and hope in the irascible. Henry's better argument is that fear and hope, the latter a kind of election and not mere desire, exist in the will. So irascible acts are in the will, though not as passions.
claims: The intellect-appetite analogy would wrongly collapse the sensitive appetite into one power.
Aristotle counts the will as rational by participation.
Hope is irascible but does not repel, refuting the rest/repel account.
Irascible acts such as fear and hope exist in the will, though not as passions.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1673.summary: Presents the reasoning of the proponent of the second opinion (Henry) that in the will they are forces, not powers. Things that differ in both mode of acting and mode of being acted on are distinct powers. Those that differ in only one are not. In the sensitive appetite, the soul acts in desiring and is acted on in anger, because the sensitive appetite moves and is moved. The will is a mover that is not moved, so there the two differ only in mode of acting and are forces, not powers.
claims: Powers differ by both mode of acting and mode of being acted on.
In the sensitive appetite the soul acts in desiring and is acted on in anger.
The will is an unmoved mover, so the irascible and concupiscible differ in it only as forces.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1715.summary: Second argument for the second opinion. When one thing arises from another and is ordered to it, they are two forces, not two powers. In the will, irascible acts arise from concupiscible acts and are ordered to them: one is angry because one desires, and repels so that the concupiscible may delight. Animals fight over food, mating or nests.
claims: What arises from and is ordered to another is a force, not a distinct power.
Irascible acts arise from and serve concupiscible acts.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1744.summary: Against the second opinion. Aureol sees no difference between forces and powers: the philosophers call the vegetative, sensitive and intellective forces, yet they are powers. If 'force' means the ultimate of a power, the act at its highest degree of straining, the irascible is not that, since hope is not the ultimate of a power. If powers are relations, two acts mean two relations and thus distinct powers. If 'force' marks acts of different kinds, that is what Aureol calls a power.
claims: There is no real difference between a force and a power.
Hope is not the ultimate degree of a power.
Acts of different kinds imply distinct powers.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1777.summary: Against the reasons for the second opinion. The argument from Aristotle fails, since the vegetative and nutritive differ more than the agent and possible intellect, yet the inference about them would be false. The argument from origin fails: if 'arising' means arising in being, it is false, since Henry himself posited only a distinction of things.
claims: Inference from degree of difference to type of distinction is invalid.
The irascible does not arise from the concupiscible in being.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1803.summary: Further reply and statement of Aureol's position. If one power presupposes another because one object presupposes another, the major premise is false. Taken as foundation, it is also false, since some such things still differ as powers. So the irascible and concupiscible are less distinct in the rational appetite than in the sensitive, yet are still two powers. He announces three conclusions.
claims: Presupposition of one object by another does not prevent distinct powers.
Irascible and concupiscible are less distinct in the rational than in the sensitive appetite, yet are two powers.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1823.summary: States the three conclusions: (1) the irascible and concupiscible are distinguished as two powers in the sensitive appetite; (2) they are also distinguished as two powers in the intellective appetite (the print repeats 'in sensitivo' by mistake); (3) they are less distinct in the intellective than in the sensitive appetite.
claims: They are two powers in the sensitive appetite.
They are two powers in the intellective appetite.
They are less distinct in the intellective than in the sensitive appetite.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1837.summary: Proof of the first conclusion. Acts that require different sensible qualities and complexions require different powers. Following Averroes, vital acts are not elicited through qualities but require bodily dispositions, as sight requires the glacial humour and hearing implanted air. Sensitive memory requires cold and dryness, imagination warm spirits. The acts of the two groups require different bodily complexions: a soft body is apt for delight, while fighting and anger require heat and dryness. So they belong to different organs and powers, like sight and hearing.
claims: Acts requiring different bodily qualities and complexions belong to different organs and powers.
Delight and anger require different bodily complexions.
Therefore irascible and concupiscible are distinct powers in the sensitive appetite.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1920.summary: Answers an objection from Averroes (De anima III) that delight and anger are in the same subject. Perhaps both are in one place, as taste and touch are both in the tongue yet have distinct organs and complexions. The printed 'Hoc de prima quaestione' refers to the first conclusion.
claims: Two powers may be co-located yet have distinct organs, as touch and taste in the tongue.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1940.summary: Proof of the second conclusion. Vital acts that do not require different bodily qualities are distinguished by their intentional mode toward the object and by the object. Understanding is a movement of the thing inward, placing the object in 'formed being'. Willing is a movement toward the thing, placing it in 'transformed' being. These are the general intentional modes to which all other acts reduce. All acts of intellect share one mode and need no distinct power. When acts have different objects and different modes of being borne, they belong to different powers. Acts that differ only by specific aspects, such as hoping and daring, need not.
claims: Inorganic vital acts are distinguished by intentional mode and object.
Understanding places its object in formed being; willing is borne toward the thing.
Different modes of being borne toward different objects ground distinct powers.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e1992.summary: Continues the proof. Contrary acts such as fearing and daring, hoping and despairing belong to one power. Lacking an organ, inorganic powers must be distinguished by a mode in genus, that is, by degree of vitality. The whole irascible group has one generic mode of relating to its object, raising up, and the concupiscible group another, being borne simply. Their object-aspects also differ: the good draws, the arduous provokes rising. So by object-aspect and mode of acting, they are distinct powers in the will.
claims: Contraries such as fear and daring belong to one power.
Inorganic powers are distinguished by a generic mode of vitality.
The good draws while the arduous provokes rising; the two are distinct powers in the will.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e2034.summary: Reply to the objection that the irascible requires the arduous good. Goodness and arduousness are two aspects. Hope and despair concern a desired good, the one rising and the other cast down. Fear and daring concern a hated evil. Anger concerns an evil already suffered and presupposes sorrow. So goodness is presupposed, not the irascible's object-aspect.
claims: Goodness and arduousness are distinct aspects.
Anger concerns an evil already experienced and presupposes sorrow.
Goodness is presupposed but is not the irascible's object-aspect.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e2056.summary: Third conclusion. In the sensitive appetite the irascible and concupiscible differ in three ways: vital mode, object-aspect and organ. In the intellective appetite they differ in only two, since there is no organ. So they are less distinct in the intellective appetite.
claims: In the sensitive appetite they differ by vital mode, object-aspect and organ.
In the intellective appetite they differ only by vital mode and object-aspect.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e2073.summary: Remarks that the reasons given for the third conclusion are on Aureol's side.

olm8ij-g52840-d1e2078.summary: Final reply to the other position. The inference from organ-based distinction fails. In all cognitive powers, judging and placing the object in formed being are the same mode. Senses are distinguished because their species are received differently, with organs of different kinds (the eye needs a transparent medium, the ear breakable air). In the intellective appetite, powers are distinguished by different modes, being drawn and being raised. The question ends here.
claims: Sensory powers are distinguished by different reception of species and organs.
In the intellective appetite, powers are distinguished by the modes of being drawn and being raised.

olm8ij-g52840-Dd1e179.summary: Article 1 establishes, by authority alone, that the irascible and concupiscible are distinguished in some way. It cites Avicenna's branches of the appetitive power (the irascible to conquer, the concupiscible to desire), Damascene's use of Aristotle's division of the soul, and the pseudo-Augustinian De spiritu et anima.
claims: The irascible and concupiscible are distinguished in some way.

olm8ij-g52840-Dd1e238.summary: Article 2 asks what distinguishes the irascible from the concupiscible. Aureol rejects five accounts. (1) Inclining versus resisting fails, since a natural form inclines and resists by one power and anger is not the irascible's defining act. (2) Simple good versus arduous good, the common view, fails because the concupiscible desires arduous goods such as beatitude and anger can target trivial evils. (3) Intensity versus remissness fails, since degree does not change species and hope is separable from intense desire. (4) Good versus evil is the weakest. (5) Naming from a defining act fails because anger is not predicated of every irascible act. Aureol's own account: powers are distinguished by irreducible general modes that unify coordinated groups of acts. The irascible group (anger, hope, despair, daring, fear) differs from the concupiscible group (love, desire, delight, hatred, flight, sorrow) in three ways. Its formal mode is rising up or straining (assurgere, conari), not mere appetition: hope is separable from desire, as when one still desires the papacy after despairing of it. Its object-aspect is arduousness, understood as what is attainable only with difficulty relative to the desirer. In causal order, every irascible act includes a prior concupiscible act, as willing includes understanding. So the powers are distinguished by mode, straining versus being borne simply, not by object alone.
claims: None of the five standard accounts of the distinction is adequate.
Powers are distinguished by irreducible general modes unifying coordinated groups of acts.
Irascible acts are formally acts of rising up or straining, not of appetition.
The arduous is what is attainable only with difficulty relative to the one desiring.
Every irascible act includes a concupiscible act.
The irascible and concupiscible are distinguished by mode: straining versus being borne simply.

olm8ij-g52840-Dd1e1162.summary: Article 3 asks where the irascible and concupiscible are distinguished, in the sensitive appetite, the intellective appetite, or both, and whether as distinct powers. Aureol reviews and refutes two opinions. The first, of an 'ancient doctor', holds them to be powers in the sensitive appetite but present in the will only by likeness. Its arguments are: a power with a general object is not divided by special aspects; the will relates to sensitive appetites as intellect to senses; the traditional division applies only to what is rational by participation; and resting versus repelling require distinct organs. Aureol replies that only aspects contained per se under the general object leave a power undivided, and arduousness is not per se under the good. The analogy would also collapse the sensitive appetite into one power. Aristotle counts the will as rational by participation. Hope is irascible yet does not repel. The second opinion, Henry of Ghent's, holds them to be powers in the sensitive appetite but only forces (vires) in the will. Aureol finds no real difference between a force and a power. His conclusions: they are two powers in the sensitive appetite, because their acts require different bodily complexions and organs. They are also two powers in the intellective appetite, because they have different intentional modes (being drawn versus being raised) and object-aspects (good versus arduous). But they are less distinct in the intellective appetite, which lacks the organic difference.
claims: The irascible and concupiscible are distinct powers in the sensitive appetite, by distinct complexions and organs.
They are also distinct powers in the intellective appetite, by intentional mode and object-aspect.
They are less distinct in the intellective than in the sensitive appetite.
There is no real distinction between a force (vis) and a power (potentia).
Irascible acts such as hope and fear exist in the will, though not as passions.

olm8ij-g52840.summary: Question 2 of Aureol's commentary on Book III, Distinction 23 asks whether the irascible and concupiscible are distinct powers, especially in the rational appetite. Aureol first notes that authorities agree they are distinguished. He then rejects five accounts of what distinguishes them (inclining versus resisting, simple versus arduous good, intensity, good versus evil, naming from a defining act). His own theory: powers are distinguished by irreducible general modes unifying coordinated groups of acts. Irascible acts (anger, hope, fear, daring, despair) are formally acts of rising up or straining toward an arduous object, attainable only with difficulty, and always presuppose a concupiscible act of desire. Against an 'ancient doctor' who places the distinction only in the sensitive appetite, and Henry of Ghent who reduces it in the will to two forces of one power, Aureol concludes that they are two powers in both appetites. In the sensitive appetite this rests on distinct organs and complexions. In the will it rests on distinct intentional modes (being drawn versus being raised) and object-aspects. They are, however, less distinct in the will.
claims: The irascible and concupiscible are distinguished by mode of tending (straining versus being borne simply), not by object alone.
Irascible acts are formally acts of rising up toward the arduous.
The arduous is what is attainable with difficulty relative to the desirer.
The irascible and concupiscible are distinct powers in both the sensitive and intellective appetites, though less distinct in the latter.
